personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Lockhart is a compulsive self-promoter whose every utterance loops back to his own fame, appearance, or achievement. His speech patterns are distinctive: he repeats names theatrically ('Harry, Harry, Harry'), pivots any topic to himself, delivers unsolicited condescending advice as though he is the patient adult and the student the lucky beneficiary, and cannot resist ranking his accomplishments (five-time Witch Weekly winner, Order of Merlin Third Class). He is also simultaneously oblivious and calculating — genuinely not registering when he is humiliating others, while also being shrewd enough to plan Memory Charms as an escape route. His emotional tone is relentless cheer that collapses instantly under real pressure. He is not merely vain; the books build a pattern of small cruelties masked as generosity (using Harry as a photo prop, taking over Sprout's lesson, closing the greenhouse door in her face). His voice has rhythm and texture: long, self-congratulatory clauses, sudden warmth that is entirely performative, and a specific brand of condescension toward everyone around him. His cowardice is present but concealed behind bravado throughout most of the book; only at the Chamber crisis does it fully surface.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core of the character: the blinding smile, the self-referential patter ('Fame's a fickle friend, Harry. Celebrity is as celebrity does'), the theatrical introductions, the catastrophic pixie lesson, the disastrous arm-deboning, the cowardly flight from Hogwarts, and the confession of fraud. Kenneth Branagh plays him with the same performative warmth and oblivious grandiosity. However, the film loses several behavioural layers that the books build through repetition. The classroom quiz — now excluded from the theatrical release — was Lockhart's single most efficient characterisation scene: it showed not just vanity but the specific mechanism of his fraud (treating students as an audience rather than pupils) and his genuine delight in his own trivia. Its absence removes a major beat. The greenhouse condescension scene (Scene 52–66 in books) is not in the film corpus. The detention fan-mail scene is present but abbreviated and loses the extended pattern of Harry's silent suffering, which in the books is where we hear Lockhart's most characteristic phrases about celebrity at greatest length. The book also shows him giving Harry unsolicited advice about fame-seeking ('You got onto the front page of the paper with me and you couldn't wait to do it again'), which reveals a specific self-serving interpretive lens he applies to everyone — the film does not replicate this pattern. The dueling club scene is largely intact. The retreat/confession scene is largely intact and is one of his most complex moments; the film preserves it nearly verbatim.
personality_voice.difference: The most significant personality loss is the removal of the quiz scene (per the exclusion note), which stripped out the clearest demonstration of how Lockhart relates to his students as an audience for his own celebrity. The greenhouse scene — where he closes the door in Sprout's face and delivers condescending advice about her own subject — is entirely absent in the film corpus, removing a specific pattern of casual, cheerful cruelty. The extended detention scene, while present, loses the rhythmic accumulation of celebrity maxims and Harry's grinding misery. The pattern of Lockhart co-opting Harry for publicity (the Flourish and Blotts scene is present, but the subsequent corridor hijacking with Colin Creevey is absent from the film corpus), which shows that his exploitation of Harry is a repeated habit rather than a single incident, is underrepresented.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — vain, fraudulent, cowardly, relentlessly self-referential — is present and recognisable. The fraud confession and Memory Charm attempt are fully intact. However, several scenes that built the specific texture of his voice (quiz, greenhouse, prolonged fan-mail patter, repeated Harry co-option) are absent or truncated, removing the cumulative behavioural pattern that makes him more than a one-note joke. This warrants a penalty from the top range but not a severe one, since the essential traits survive. Score range 14–17 is appropriate — character remains recognisable but important textural traits and some secondary behaviours are reduced.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Lockhart serves multiple narrative functions simultaneously: comic relief, plot driver (his incompetence creates problems, his fan mail detention is where Harry hears the voice for the first time), false authority figure who delays and misdirects the investigation, and finally a structural catalyst whose cowardice and fraud are fully exposed. He also provides world-building texture — his books are everywhere, his celebrity is a lens through which Rowling examines wizard popular culture. He is active in the plot at key moments: he physically intervenes at the dueling club (disastrously), he attempts to deboneHarry, he misleads McGonagall about the danger passing, he volunteers for the Chamber and then tries to flee. His agency is mostly destructive or negative, but it is genuine agency: he makes choices that change the situation, usually for the worse. Crucially, he is the one who reveals the full extent of his fraud to Harry and Ron (the confession scene), and it is his attempted Memory Charm — using Ron's broken wand — that causes the cave-in separating the boys.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves his core narrative functions. The fan-mail detention as the setting for Harry first hearing the voice is present. The dueling club is present with his disastrous intervention with the snake. The deboning of Harry's arm is present. The fraud confession is present. The attempted Memory Charm and its backfiring are present. His misleading the school about danger having passed (book Scene 278–280) is not shown in the film corpus. His repeated classroom reenactments using Harry as prop (book Scene 193–198) are absent from the film corpus. His Valentine's Day spectacle (book Scene 281–288) is absent. His cheerful dismissal of Hagrid's guilt (book Scene 300–320) is absent.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The most significant agency loss is the absence of the class reenactment scenes, where Lockhart uses Harry as a performing prop across multiple lessons — this is a sustained pattern of active (if absurd) agency. The Valentine's Day scene, where he unilaterally redecorates the school and commandeers teachers, is absent — this shows Lockhart exercising institutional authority without permission and imposing on others. His self-satisfied commentary to McGonagall that he has personally ended the danger (book Scene 278–280) is absent; this is a moment where his agency actively misdirects the investigation. However, all the structurally critical moments of his narrative role are preserved.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The film keeps the most plot-significant agency beats intact. The absent scenes (reenactments, Valentine's Day, false danger-has-passed commentary) reduce the texture of his ongoing negative agency in the school but do not change his essential narrative function. Score range 14–17 is appropriate — role and agency are reduced but recognisable.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Lockhart's motivation is unusually simple for a supporting character but executed with precision: he wants fame, adulation, and wealth, and he has built his entire identity on a lie that he is too committed to abandon. His internal conflict, such as it is, is not moral — he has already resolved it entirely in favour of self-interest. What the books show is a character whose motivation is so totalising that it overrides any instinct of self-preservation (he keeps performing competence even when it is obviously going to fail), professional duty (he abandons his post the moment it becomes dangerous), and basic human decency (he planned to wipe the memories of two children to protect his book sales). The fraud confession scene makes his motivation explicit: 'My books wouldn't have sold half as well if people didn't think I'd done all those things.' The Memory Charm is not an impulsive act of panic — it is calculated. He has done this before, to everyone he stole credit from.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves this motivation with high fidelity. The fraud confession is nearly word-for-word from the book. The Memory Charm attempt and its rationale ('I'm rather gifted with Memory Charms. Otherwise, you see, all those wizards would've gone blabbing and I'd never have sold another book') is present. The film adds a slightly more elaborate justification in the confession ('There was work involved. I had to track these people down... You want fame, you have to be prepared for a long, hard slog') that is also book-accurate. His motivation is as clearly stated in the film as in the books.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Minimal. The film loses some contextual scenes that reinforce the motivation through repeated behaviour (the quiz, the reenactments, the Valentine's Day display), but the motivation itself is not changed or obscured. The explicit confession scene is the primary evidence for his motivation and it is fully intact.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified only in the sense that fewer scenes establish them through accumulation; the core statement is fully present. This is compression without change — the score should not be heavily penalised. Score range 11–13 is appropriate given slight loss of reinforcing context.

character_arc.book_baseline: Lockhart's arc is a sustained deflation. He begins at peak celebrity, is gradually undermined by his own incompetence (pixies, deboning, dueling club failure), passes through a false plateau of self-delusion (insisting he has solved the Chamber mystery), and ends in complete exposure and self-inflicted amnesia. The arc's final stage — St Mungo's in Book 5, where he is encountered still signing autographs, now for no reason he can remember — is the darkest coda: fame without identity, performance without purpose, vanity as the only surviving instinct. His arc is not a redemption arc; it is an unmasking arc, moving from false authority to revealed fraud to physical dissolution of selfhood. The Book 5 hospital scene is the arc's endpoint — it confirms the amnesia is permanent and shows, with grim comedy, that even without memory he performs the same gestures.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film covers the core arc: celebrity introduction, repeated incompetence, exposure, Memory Charm backfire, and final vacancy. The Chamber sequence and its aftermath are intact. However, the Book 5 St Mungo's scene does not appear in the film corpus — it was not adapted in any Harry Potter film. This means the darkest and most thematically resonant endpoint of the arc is absent. In the film, Lockhart's arc ends with him being led away by Dumbledore, smiling blankly ('Am I a professor? Goodness. I expect I was hopeless, was I?'). This captures the immediate aftermath but not the long-term confirmation that the amnesia is permanent, that he has been institutionalised, and that the performance instinct (autographs, fan mail) persists without any actual self behind it.
character_arc.difference: The arc's culminating beat — the St Mungo's scene — is absent. This is a Book 5 scene and would have been in a different film (Order of the Phoenix), but its absence means the arc is incomplete: the full cost of his choices (permanent institutionalisation, his only surviving instinct being the hollow performance of celebrity) is not shown.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is present through its main stages and the immediate aftermath of the Memory Charm is well-handled. The absence of the St Mungo's scene is a genuine loss of the arc's resolution, but it belongs to a different film — penalising too heavily for material that was never within the scope of the Chamber of Secrets film would be unfair. The arc as adapted in the Chamber of Secrets film is compressed but faithful. Score range 11–13 is appropriate.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Lockhart's most important relationships are: (1) Harry — whom he exploits as a fame-amplifier and photo prop throughout the year, culminating in his attempted Memory Charm against him; (2) Hermione — his most devoted fan, whose admiration he registers with genuine pleasure and exploits for classroom purposes; (3) the other teachers, especially Sprout and McGonagall — whom he condescends to, co-opts, and is finally exposed by when they collectively call his bluff in the staffroom; (4) the general student body — his audience, whose attention he manages constantly. The staffroom confrontation (book Scenes 322–336) is one of the best relationship moments in the book: the teachers have quietly despised him all year and now collectively set the trap that exposes him.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry relationship is present in its key beats (Flourish and Blotts, detention, fraud confession, Memory Charm attempt). The Hermione relationship is present but reduced — the film shows Hermione's admiration (reading his books, defending him after the pixie lesson, keeping his get-well card under her pillow) but loses the specific scene where Lockhart singles her out in class with warm approval and she manipulates this to get the Restricted Section note. The teacher relationships are mostly intact in the staffroom scene, though several of the smaller prior incidents (closing the greenhouse door in Sprout's face, condescending to McGonagall in the corridor) are absent from the film corpus. The student-as-audience relationship loses the extended classroom reenactment scenes and the Valentine's Day spectacle.
key_relationships.difference: The Hermione dynamic loses a key beat: the Restricted Section scene shows Lockhart using his approval of Hermione as currency and Hermione manipulating his vanity right back — a moment that reveals the transactional, slightly mutual quality of their dynamic, and is the one scene where Hermione is shown to be sharp-eyed about Lockhart even while admiring him. The teacher relationships lose the greenhouse condescension scene, which establishes the pattern that makes their staffroom revenge satisfying.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Core relationship dynamics are preserved (Harry as exploited prop, Hermione as devoted fan, teachers as eventual exposers). The absent scenes reduce the texture and complexity of these dynamics but do not reverse them. The Hermione-Lockhart dynamic in particular loses an important nuance. Score range 7–8 is appropriate — mostly faithful with some compression.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Lockhart's complexity comes from several sources: (1) The gap between his genuinely organised, premeditated fraud and his bumbling performance of competence — he is not merely stupid; he is intelligent in specific self-serving ways. (2) The quiz scene (now excluded from theatrical release) — which showed a character who has made himself the entire curriculum, treating students' education as a vehicle for his self-promotion. (3) The extended classroom reenactment pattern — where Harry is used as a prop across multiple sessions, building a sustained portrait of exploitation normalised as pedagogy. (4) The Valentine's Day scene — where he unilaterally imposes his ego on the entire school, commandeers colleagues, and is oblivious to their collective contempt. (5) The greenhouse scene — where cheerful condescension to Sprout shows he treats all colleagues as lesser. (6) His self-satisfied commentary after each failure (dueling club, deboning), always finding a way to reframe disaster as deliberate instruction. (7) The St Mungo's scene — where his only surviving instinct is celebrity performance, now entirely detached from any self.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The quiz scene is excluded from theatrical release per the scoring instruction — this is a direct loss of one of the richest characterisation scenes. The classroom reenactments are absent. The Valentine's Day scene is absent. The greenhouse condescension scene is absent. The St Mungo's scene is absent (different film). What remains are the Flourish and Blotts scene, the pixie lesson, the fan-mail detention, the arm-deboning, the dueling club, and the Chamber crisis. These are the highest-drama beats and they are well-executed, but they represent the peaks of his arc rather than the sustained everyday texture that makes the peaks meaningful.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film loses: the quiz (his most concentrated self-satirising scene, now excluded), the classroom reenactments (sustained exploitation of Harry as prop), the Valentine's Day takeover (institutional ego unchecked), the greenhouse condescension (habitual treatment of colleagues), and the St Mungo's endpoint (arc resolution). What survives is the skeleton of the character — the most plot-necessary scenes — without much of the flesh that made the book characterisation rich and uncomfortable.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The excluded quiz scene alone is significant — it was the scene most precisely designed to show the mechanism of his fraud as applied to education. The other absent scenes (reenactments, Valentine's Day, greenhouse) collectively represent the sustained everyday Lockhart that gives context and texture to the big moments. The character is recognisable in the film but substantially flattened: he functions as a plot device and comic foil rather than the fully developed satirical portrait the books construct. This warrants a score in the 8–10 range — noticeable simplification, important nuances and repeated patterns missing.

score_caps_applied: Cap 1 (85): Not triggered — the film does not remove a major part of his complexity while keeping the rest superficially faithful at a level that would inflate the score above 85. The losses are significant but the total score is already below this threshold.
Cap 4 (70): Considered — the film preserves considerably more than the 'broad identity' of the character, including the key confession, Memory Charm, and Chamber scenes, so this cap is not triggered.
Score naturally lands at 72 based on dimensional scoring; no cap adjustments required beyond the natural scoring.
comparative.key_observations: The film adaptation of Lockhart is faithful in its highest-stakes moments — the fraud confession, the Memory Charm attempt, the Chamber crisis — and captures his defining traits of performative vanity, cowardice, and compulsive self-promotion. Kenneth Branagh's performance delivers the core character recognisably. However, the theatrical exclusion of the classroom quiz scene, combined with the absence of the greenhouse condescension, the Valentine's Day takeover, and the sustained classroom reenactment pattern, removes the everyday texture that made the books' portrait more than a cartoon. The quiz scene in particular was the single most efficient characterisation scene Rowling wrote for him, and its exclusion from the theatrical cut is the most consequential single loss. The St Mungo's scene (Book 5) represents the lost arc resolution — the confirmation that his amnesia is permanent and that celebrity performance is his only surviving instinct — but this belongs to a different film. The result is a Lockhart who works as a plot device and provides the required comic beats, but is missing the sustained satirical portrait of fraudulent celebrity that the books construct through accumulation. Recognisable, but not fully faithful.
